thesis: Software functionality, expressive implementation, interoperability and licensing require distinct legal and engineering analyses.
role: Apply filtering, provenance and separate release gates to software.

ideas.statement: Filter functional constraints and conventional elements before comparing protectable implementation; assets, patents, secrets and contracts remain separate.
SAS and Google v. Oracle reach different scoped conclusions; clean-room practice and lawful specifications support evidence without providing blanket immunity.
Open-source permissions carry version- and use-specific terms; rewriting headers neither removes obligations nor attaches a licence to every independent equivalent function.
Behavioral equivalence, legal independence and security require separate tests; matching, SBOMs and signatures support evidence but do not establish title.
Software production includes reliability, migration, maintenance and support; legitimate service value differs from trapping customers.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Altai is a jurisdiction-specific judicial method; unrestricted equivalence undecidability leaves bounded verification useful, and clean rooms do not neutralize other rights.
